justifications.decision: The printed yotsya before iti is explained by final e of yotsye becoming ay before initial i; iti marks the preceding words as quoted speech. The verb is therefore first-person singular future from yudh, negated by na.
options_considered: Take yotsya as the pausal verbal form as printed
Restore pausal yotsye before iti and construe it as first-person future direct speech
justifications.chosen: na yotsya iti is understood as sandhi for na yotsye iti, a direct quotation: “I shall not fight.”

justifications.decision: With the absolutive of vac, the accusative names mark the person to whom speech is directed: first “having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa,” then “having said ‘I shall not fight’ to Govinda.” Both names refer to Kṛṣṇa.
options_considered: Treat the accusatives as bare objects, ‘having spoken Hṛṣīkeśa/Govinda’
Treat the accusatives as addressed persons, ‘having spoken/said to Hṛṣīkeśa/Govinda’
justifications.chosen: hṛṣīkeśam and govindam are accusatives of the person addressed with the two occurrences of uktvā.

justifications.decision: tūṣṇīm is an indeclinable meaning “silently, in silence,” construed with babhūva from bhū; ha is an emphatic or narrative particle, lightly represented by “indeed.”
options_considered: Take tūṣṇīm as an accusative noun object
Take tūṣṇīm as an indeclinable complement/adverb with bhū
justifications.chosen: tūṣṇīṃ babhūva ha means “became silent indeed.”

evidence.translation: No commentary is supplied for this unit; this decision rests on grammar and the dictionary entries for tūṣṇīm and bhū.

justifications.decision: The dictionary entries identify the former three as names of Kṛṣṇa or Arjuna, while paraṃtapa is a transparent descriptive adjective, “destroying foes.” Since commentary is absent, no special etymological interpretation of the names is built into the translation.
options_considered: Etymologically translate all names and epithets
Retain established proper names and translate only the transparent descriptive epithet
justifications.chosen: Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, and Govinda are retained as proper names; parantapaḥ is translated as the descriptive epithet “foe-scorcher.”

translation:
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the foe-scorcher (parantapaḥ),
having said to Govinda, “I shall not fight,”
became silent indeed.
one_shot_delta: Because the commentary is silent, the main risk is grammatical rather than commentarial: a translation could miss that printed yotsya iti represents pausal yotsye iti, “I shall not fight.”
A translation could import a vocative parantapa from another reading; the supplied unit reads parantapaḥ, so this apparatus treats it as a nominative epithet of Guḍākeśaḥ.
A translation could render hṛṣīkeśam and govindam as two separate direct objects rather than as names of Kṛṣṇa functioning as the addressee with uktvā.
open_questions: No commentary is supplied for this unit. The supplied unit reads nominative parantapaḥ; if an edition read vocative parantapa, the construal and translation of that word would change.
